output.title: Design dashboards so neglect is visible quickly
output.body:
Dashboard neglect is usually not a software problem first. It is a control problem: there is a screen, report, or approval view that should guide a recurring decision, but nobody checks it often enough to keep the work moving. For a small business, the useful question is not whether AI can read the dashboard. It is what happens when the owner does not look at it for two days.

One bounded way to design against that is to separate three responses. First, add a reminder if the owner simply forgets. Second, automate the data refresh so the dashboard stays current without manual copy-paste. Third, only if the rule is clear, automate the handoff of the next step while keeping human approval in place for money movement and other high-risk decisions. Human approval stays the gate.

A practical next step is to pick one dashboard the business already relies on and write one plain-English rule for it: what input arrives, what status changes, and what action follows. If the rule is fuzzy, automation should stop at data collection. If the rule is clear, the pilot stays narrow and tests whether the need is a reminder, a refresh, or a workflow handoff. That is Bareni’s policy: work inside the customer’s own accounts and tools, with no-lock-in positioning, not a promise of magic.
